title: Physics, Book IV, Parts 10-13 (time)
version: Hardie and Gaye translation, MIT Internet Classics Archive copy; page ends in Part 13, Part 14 absent from the copy
locators: Parts 10 (puzzles about the now, rejection of time as heaven's motion), 11 (time and change, number of motion by before and after, the now as unit), 12 (time as measure, rest measured indirectly, same time everywhere at once), 13 (the now as link and limit, time does not fail while motion exists)
assumptions: Time is not motion but not independent of it; before and after hold first in magnitude; one time everywhere
conclusion: Time is the number of motion in respect of before and after; time and motion are mutually defining; no time unless some motion exists
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Whether the thesis concerns existence or awareness; whether it allows changeless time (Coope 2001, lead only)
relevance: Anchor for the Aristotelian and relational tradition against which the local-clock note is read
limits: Translation, not the Greek; Part 14 (counting requires a soul) not read; no commentary read; Parts 10 and 12 read in part

title: Confessions, Book XI (time and eternity)
version: J.G. Pilkington translation (as stated on the page), New Advent copy
locators: Chapter 14 section 17 (God made time; what is time), 18-20 sections 26 (three presents), 24-27 sections 30-31 (time not the motion of a body, rest is measured), 33, 36-38 (measuring in the mind, the psalm), 41 (God's knowing)
assumptions: Past and future do not exist; time is measurable through a present of memory, attention and expectation
conclusion: Time is not body motion; it is measured in the mind; God is outside time
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Whether the view is a psychological theory of time or only of its measure
relevance: Historical position; the sun-stands-still passage is an early separation of time from body motion
limits: Selected sections only (about a quarter of the book); translation; no commentary read

title: Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, Scholium to the Definitions (absolute and relative time and space)
version: Motte translation (1729) as reprinted in the 1846 edition, Wikisource transcription
locators: Scholium, definitions I and II (absolute and relative time and space) and the paragraph on astronomical equation: there may be no equable motion; duration persists whether motions are swift, slow or none
assumptions: Absolute time exists independently of anything external; sensible measures by motion approximate it
conclusion: Time flows equably of itself; true time is distinguished from its measures
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Whether absolute time is needed for dynamics (hole argument literature, not read)
relevance: Primary source of the substantival side; the 'or none at all' clause is Newton's own statement of changeless duration
limits: Translation via a transcription; the bucket and rotating-globes arguments not read; SEP Newton downloaded but not read

title: Exchange of papers between Leibniz and Clarke
version: Jonathan Bennett's abridged modernisation (2017); PDF text extracted with a short local script
locators: Leibniz 3 (the shift argument for time, order of successions, absolute space as idol), Clarke 3 (time and space are quantities, order is not), Clarke 4 start; Leibniz 4 (indiscernibles) in part
assumptions: Principle of sufficient reason; identity of indiscernibles
conclusion: Time as an order of successions; shifted-world indiscernibility; Clarke's reply from divine will
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Modern substantivalist replies to the shift argument (not read)
relevance: Primary source of the relational side and of its canonical argument
limits: Bennett omits and rewrites; this is not Leibniz's wording; read in excerpts, not in full; Papers 1, 2 and 5 not read

title: Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Aesthetic, Section II (time), sections 5-7
locators: Section 5 points 1-5 (metaphysical exposition), 6 (transcendental exposition), 7 (conclusions a-c, empirical reality and transcendental ideality)
assumptions: Time is a priori; coexistence and succession presuppose it
conclusion: Time is the form of inner sense, empirically real, transcendentally ideal
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Relation of the Kantian view to relativistic time (not read)
relevance: Completes the historical set; point 2 says time void of phenomena can be represented, which bears on changeless time
limits: Translation; Aesthetic only; the Analogies (time, causation, permanence) not read; no commentary read

title: The Unreality of Time
version: Mind 17 (1908) 456-473, ditext.com transcription (not collated against the journal)
locators: Opening (A, B series), change and the A series, incompatibility of past, present, future, the vicious-circle reply, plurality of time series
assumptions: Time involves change; change requires the A series
conclusion: The A series is contradictory, so time is unreal
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Replies by B-theorists and by relational A-theories (other lanes)
relevance: Source of the 'index' dilemma that main.tex Part IV echoes
limits: Selected passages only; transcription; the tense-and-language lane covers the later debate

title: Time without Change
version: Journal of Philosophy 66(12) (19 June 1969) 363-381; JSTOR scan on a third-party university course page (not a publisher or author copy); text extracted with a local script, pages out of order
locators: pp. 367-368 (cause of a freeze's end, awareness during changeless interval), 371 (grounds for believing, footnote 7 on relational change), 373 (simplicity argument, verification), 379-380 (McTaggartian predicates, Barcan Marcus's observation)
assumptions: Possible worlds with different laws are admissible; simplicity governs induction
conclusion: It is conceivable that people could have good grounds for believing in changeless intervals and measuring them
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Warmbrod's cause-of-restart objection; Le Poidevin 2010 (both leads, not read)
relevance: Main source in the time-without-change debate
limits: Provenance of the copy is not authorised; pp. 363-366, 369-370, 372, 374-378 skimmed only; relativity discussion on p. 369 not read

title: Relationism about Time and Temporal Vacua
relevance: Relationist reply to Shoemaker: relationism need not require change, actual or possible

title: On the physical basis of cosmic time
locators: Abstract; Section 1; Section 2.2 'The time-clock relation and relationism' (Aristotle, Leibniz, Grunbaum, Smolin, Barbour)
assumptions: Time concept requires a possible physical process (clock core); time order has a physical basis if a process could occur between A and B
conclusion: Non-reductive relationism tied to clocks; cosmic time lacks a physical basis before the electroweak transition
proof_status: Philosophical argument; not a formal proof
open_questions: Whether the principle survives for time order without a clock process
relevance: Closest source to the local-clock note's conclusion, in the Aristotelian and relational tradition
limits: Read only the abstract, introduction and Section 2.2 (about a fifth); sections on the early universe not read; preprint, published version not checked; text extraction had gaps
